analysis.one_liner: Bans AI chatbots from using addictive design features on users under 18 and funds research on their mental health effects.
analysis.headline: The bill, introduced with four Democratic cosponsors on July 27, 2026, was referred to two House committees and has had no hearings, markup, or vote since.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would create an interagency task force to study how AI chatbots' addictive design features affect young people's mental health, and would have HHS fund university research ($3 million) and outreach to parents and teachers ($5 million). It would force AI chatbot companies to hand over data to researchers, with fines up to $10 million for refusing, and would make it illegal to offer a chatbot with addictive design features — like mimicking a real person, building an emotional bond, or using tricks to keep a user engaged — to anyone under 18, with a $5,000 fine per violation.
analysis.who_benefits: Minors who use AI chatbots, and their families. The bill aims to shield them from chatbots designed to build emotional attachment and maximize engagement, and would give parents and teachers training to spot warning signs of unhealthy use.

how_it_helps.text: Prohibits covered entities from making AI chatbots with addictive design features available to youth, enforceable by the Attorney General with civil penalties and injunctions.

Funds university research on chatbots' effects on youth mental health ($3 million authorized for fiscal years 2027-2032) and outreach grants to nonprofits and community groups to train parents and teachers to recognize warning signs ($5 million).

Requires chatbot companies to give researchers access to data on how their products affect young users, with fines up to $10 million per violation for noncompliance, and requires identifiable information to be removed before sharing.

analysis.who_pays: AI chatbot companies, which would face compliance costs, mandatory data sharing, and civil penalties, and would have to build age verification — which collects users' age data, though the bill requires deleting it within 24 hours.

drawbacks.text: The definition of 'addictive design feature' is sweeping: it includes showing typing bubbles, providing avatars, and storing information from previous conversations, so nearly any conversational AI chatbot would be barred from serving minors.

Enforcing the youth prohibition depends on age verification technology, which requires collecting age data from users — a privacy tradeoff the bill only partly mitigates by limiting data to what is strictly necessary and requiring deletion within 24 hours.

The task force's recommendations are advisory, the per-violation penalty for offering an addictive chatbot to a minor is modest at $5,000, and enforcement rests entirely on the Attorney General's discretion.
The bill's own findings acknowledge that First Amendment protections for commercial speech must be balanced against these restrictions, a tension that could invite legal challenge.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The real-world effect would be modest: most of the bill is study, grants, and recommendations, and the binding prohibition carries small per-violation fines. The youth protection provision is the substantive piece, but its broad design definitions would effectively ban most AI chatbots from serving minors, and it depends on age verification that collects some user data. The costs fall on chatbot companies; the privacy risk to users is limited but real.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced with four Democratic cosponsors in late July 2026 and referred to two House committees, where it has sat without a hearing or vote; the session ends in early January 2027.

narrative.text: Rep. Becca Balint introduced H.R. 9948 on July 27, 2026, joined by Reps. Deluzio, Suozzi, and Watson Coleman.
The bill was referred the same day to the Energy and Commerce Committee and the Education and Workforce Committee.
The bill has four cosponsors, all House Democrats, and no further action has been taken since the referrals.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: So far, AI chatbot companies, which face no new restrictions, data-sharing mandates, or penalties while the bill sits in committee with the session winding down.

sides.party_line_note: All five sponsors and cosponsors are House Democrats; no Republican has signed on, and the bill sits in two committees chaired by Republicans.

industries.industry: AI chatbot and generative AI companies
industries.note: The bill would bar them from offering chatbots with engagement-maximizing features to minors, force them to share user data with academic researchers under threat of fines up to $10 million, and expose them to $5,000 fines per violation of the youth prohibition. Their business depends on keeping users engaged, which runs directly against the bill's goal of limiting youth emotional attachment to chatbots.

The youth prohibition effectively requires chatbot makers to deploy age verification, creating demand for these providers. But the bill restricts them to collecting only the data strictly necessary to determine age and requires deletion within 24 hours, limiting their business model.

industries.industry: Mental health nonprofits and community organizations
industries.note: A $5 million outreach grant program would fund tax-exempt nonprofits and community groups to train parents and teachers to recognize warning signs of harmful chatbot use in young people.
A $3 million grant program would fund university research on chatbots' effects on youth mental health, backed by a legal right to obtain data from chatbot companies.

analysis.trajectory: The bill is roughly five months old with four cosponsors, no Republican support, and no committee action in either of the two committees it was referred to. With the 119th Congress ending January 3, 2027, the most likely path is that it dies in committee at the end of the session without a hearing or vote, and would need to be reintroduced in the next Congress.
